1. Cut 3-4 inch stem tips with sharp knife
2. Let cuttings dry in shade for 2-3 hours
3. Mix 50% potting soil + 50% perlite
4. Poke holes with pencil
5. Plant cuttings, firm soil
6. Water lightly
7. Place in bright indirect light
Roots appear in 2-3 weeks!

WHAT YOU NEED:
- Mother plant with healthy stems
- Sharp knife (utility knife or craft knife)
- 50% potting soil + 50% perlite
- Small pots (4-6 inch)
- Pencil (for making holes)

STEP-BY-STEP METHOD:

1. Take Cuttings:
   - Cut 3-4 inch stem tips from healthy growth
   - Use sharp, clean knife
   - Take cuttings in morning when plants are hydrated
   - Remove all but top 1 or 2 leaves and any flower buds
   - 6 cuttings = 2 full pots (3 per pot)

2. Dry Cuttings:
   - Let cuttings sit in shade for 2-3 hours
   - This allows cut end to callus slightly
   - Prevents rot when planted
   - Critical step - don't skip!

3. Prepare Soil Mix:
   - 50% potting soil + 50% perlite
   - Excellent drainage prevents rot
   - Fill pots to top, don't compact
   - Mix thoroughly before filling

4. Plant Cuttings:
   - Poke 3 holes per pot with pencil
   - Insert cuttings so at least one node is covered
   - Nodes = bumps on stem where leaves emerge
   - Firm soil gently around cutting
   - Space 3 cuttings evenly in each pot

5. Water & Place:
   - Water lightly to settle soil
   - Don't soak - pelargoniums hate wet feet!
   - Place in warm spot with bright indirect light
   - NOT direct sun (will stress cuttings)
   - Keep soil barely moist, not wet

TIMELINE:
- Week 1-2: Cuttings establish, may look slightly wilted (normal!)
- Week 2-3: Roots developing
- Week 3-4: New growth appears = rooting success!
- Week 6-8: Ready to pot up individually

WHEN TO TAKE CUTTINGS:
Best time: Spring or early fall
Can also do: Late summer
Avoid: Winter (slow rooting) or hottest summer months

WHY THIS METHOD WORKS:
✅ Drying prevents rot (pelargoniums are susceptible!)
✅ 50/50 mix = perfect drainage for geraniums
✅ No rooting hormone needed (geraniums root easily!)
✅ Multiple cuttings per pot = save money
✅ Soil method = stronger roots than water propagation

Perfect for Zones 9-11 where geraniums grow as perennials year-round (Southern California, Florida, Texas, Arizona, warm climates). In colder zones, propagate in spring and grow as annuals or overwinter indoors.

GERANIUM vs PELARGONIUM:
What we commonly call "geraniums" are actually pelargoniums! True geraniums are hardy perennials (cranesbill). Zonal pelargoniums (Pelargonium × hortorum) are the classic bedding "geraniums" with colorful flowers and sometimes patterned leaves.

Why propagate geraniums:
🌺 FREE plants from one mother plant
💰 Save money (geraniums can be $5-10 each!)
🌱 Preserve favorite varieties
🎁 Share with friends and neighbors
🏡 Fill containers and beds inexpensively

Zones 9-11: Grow outdoors year-round as perennials
Zones 8 and below: Grow as annuals or take cuttings in fall to overwinter indoors

Propagating geraniums is incredibly simple if you follow the right steps. From choosing the perfect node to preparing the ideal soil mix, I will guide you through the entire process so you can successfully grow new, healthy geranium plants right at home!

🛠️ Materials Needed:
- Small paper, plastic, or coffee cups (with drainage holes added)
- Well-draining soil mix (Sand, Perlite, and Coco Peat)
- Pruning shears or scissors (Sanitized!)
- A healthy mature geranium plant

💡 Key Tips for 100% Rooting Success:
- Proper Drainage is Crucial: Always ensure your cup has plenty of drainage holes. Geranium cuttings will rot quickly in soggy, waterlogged soil.
- Sanitize Your Tools: Always clean your scissors or pruners before making a cut to prevent infections and diseases from transferring to your healthy plant.
- Remove Lower Leaves: Strip the bottom leaves from your cutting, leaving only the top two. This stops the cutting from wasting energy on foliage and redirects it straight to root development.
- Plant Deeply: Make sure at least 2 to 3 node areas are buried in the soil; this is where the new roots will emerge.
- Keep Out of Direct Sun & Wind: Store your fresh cuttings in a bright area that receives plenty of indirect light, but strictly NO direct sunlight. Shield them from heavy winds to prevent the stems from loosening in the soil. Roots should develop in about a month!

Geraniums are among the easiest flowering plants to multiply. One healthy mother plant can give you 10–20 new plants every season. No seeds, no expensive saplings, just one cutting and the right technique.
🌱 What you'll learn in this video:
✅ The best time to take geranium cuttings in India
✅ How to choose a healthy stem for propagation
✅ The correct cutting length and where to cut (node method)
✅ Why you should remove lower leaves and flower buds
✅ Callusing: why drying the cut end prevents rot

✅ The best soil mix for fast rooting

✅ Watering, light and care until roots form
✅ When and how to transplant your new geranium plant
✅ Common mistakes that cause cuttings to rot
🗓️ Best season for geranium propagation in India:
February–March and September–November are ideal. Avoid the peak monsoon, when humidity causes stem rot, and extreme summer heat.
🪴 Quick method summary:
1️⃣ Take a 4–6 inch healthy, non-flowering tip cutting just below a node.
2️⃣ Remove the lower leaves, keeping only 2–3 at the top. Pinch off any buds.
3️⃣ Let the cut end dry and callus for a few hours.
4️⃣ Dip it in rooting hormone (optional).
5️⃣ Plant it in a well-draining mix of cocopeat + perlite or sand.
6️⃣ Keep it in bright, indirect light. Water lightly and avoid overwatering.
7️⃣ Roots form in about 2–4 weeks. New leaf growth means success! 🎉
⚠️ Important tip: Don't cover geranium cuttings with plastic. Unlike many plants, geraniums dislike high humidity and can rot quickly.

results.title: How to Propagate Geraniums from Cuttings - Easy Pelargonium Propagation!
results.description:
How to Propagate Geraniums from Cuttings (Step-by-Step):
1. Cut 3-4 inch stem tips with sharp knife
2. Let cuttings dry in shade for 2-3 hours
3. Mix 50% potting soil + 50% perlite
4. Poke holes with pencil
5. Plant cuttings, firm soil
6. Water lightly
7. Place in bright indirect light
Roots appear in 2-3 weeks!

WHAT YOU NEED:
- Mother plant with healthy stems
- Sharp knife (utility knife or craft knife)
- 50% potting soil + 50% perlite
- Small pots (4-6 inch)
- Pencil (for making holes)

STEP-BY-STEP METHOD:

1. Take Cuttings:
   - Cut 3-4 inch stem tips from healthy growth
   - Use sharp, clean knife
   - Take cuttings in morning when plants are hydrated
   - Remove all but top 1 or 2 leaves and any flower buds
   - 6 cuttings = 2 full pots (3 per pot)

2. Dry Cuttings:
   - Let cuttings sit in shade for 2-3 hours
   - This allows cut end to callus slightly
   - Prevents rot when planted
   - Critical step - don't skip!

3. Prepare Soil Mix:
   - 50% potting soil + 50% perlite
   - Excellent drainage prevents rot
   - Fill pots to top, don't compact
   - Mix thoroughly before filling

4. Plant Cuttings:
   - Poke 3 holes per pot with pencil
   - Insert cuttings so at least one node is covered
   - Nodes = bumps on stem where leaves emerge
   - Firm soil gently around cutting
   - Space 3 cuttings evenly in each pot

5. Water & Place:
   - Water lightly to settle soil
   - Don't soak - pelargoniums hate wet feet!
   - Place in warm spot with bright indirect light
   - NOT direct sun (will stress cuttings)
   - Keep soil barely moist, not wet

TIMELINE:
- Week 1-2: Cuttings establish, may look slightly wilted (normal!)
- Week 2-3: Roots developing
- Week 3-4: New growth appears = rooting success!
- Week 6-8: Ready to pot up individually

WHEN TO TAKE CUTTINGS:
Best time: Spring or early fall
Can also do: Late summer
Avoid: Winter (slow rooting) or hottest summer months

WHY THIS METHOD WORKS:
✅ Drying prevents rot (pelargoniums are susceptible!)
✅ 50/50 mix = perfect drainage for geraniums
✅ No rooting hormone needed (geraniums root easily!)
✅ Multiple cuttings per pot = save money
✅ Soil method = stronger roots than water propagation

Perfect for Zones 9-11 where geraniums grow as perennials year-round (Southern California, Florida, Texas, Arizona, warm climates). In colder zones, propagate in spring and grow as annuals or overwinter indoors.

GERANIUM vs PELARGONIUM:
What we commonly call "geraniums" are actually pelargoniums! True geraniums are hardy perennials (cranesbill). Zonal pelargoniums (Pelargonium × hortorum) are the classic bedding "geraniums" with colorful flowers and sometimes patterned leaves.

Why propagate geraniums:
🌺 FREE plants from one mother plant
💰 Save money (geraniums can be $5-10 each!)
🌱 Preserve favorite varieties
🎁 Share with friends and neighbors
🏡 Fill containers and beds inexpensively

Zones 9-11: Grow outdoors year-round as perennials
Zones 8 and below: Grow as annuals or take cuttings in fall to overwinter indoors
